newsitem.title: USA: Dole goes coast to coast with hits on Clinton ethics.
newsitem.headline: Dole goes coast to coast with hits on Clinton ethics.

text.p: Bob Dole completed a week-long, coast-to-coast assault on President Bill Clinton's character and ethics on Saturday as the Republican challenger tried to catch up with just 17 days left to Election Day.

Dole flew to this naval base city from Kentucky and before that the mountain states and the West Coast, at each stop pounding away at the Democratic Party for accepting money Dole said were improper donations from foreign interests seeking favours.

Underscoring the same theme at a harbourside rally, Dole said tongue-in-cheek he had been waiting for years for foreign aid to get to America. "And now it's coming and it's all going to the Democratic National Committee. Foreign aid has finally made it to America - Yeah," he yelled sarcastically.
"It's all going to re-elect President Clinton."

Dole also got in a dig at Clinton who avoided the military draft during the Vietnam War. Dole said Clinton had been AWOL (absent without leave), in the war on drugs. "He's been AWOL before and now he's AWOL on drugs." said Dole.
Dole earlier told a partisan crowd at a Somerset, Kentucky rally: "Because integrity is everything, we cannot allow political influence of any American to be outweighed by foreign money."

Dole struck out again at reports of hundreds of thousands of dollars in questionable contributions from people associated with foreign interests, including Indonesia and South Korea. He has been asking Clinton to explain the funds and has accused the administration of stonewalling the issue.
"The stonewall is beginning to tumble," said Dole as he noted the Democratic Party has relieved a party fundraiser, John Huang, who targeted Asian interests for contributions.

Clinton's state chairman, Louisville Mayor Jerry Abramson, said in a statement issued at the Dole rally: "Kentuckians do not want to hear personal attacks on the president -- they want to know why you chose to vote for (House of Representatives Speaker) Newt Gingrich's 1995 budget.

"They do not want speeches laced with tall tales and innuendo ... they want to know why you (Dole) voted against the crime bill. They do not want speeches of slander and overheated rhetoric," said Abramson.

This was a line of attack he started in California before and after his Wednesday debate with Clinton that he hopes will lift him in polls. He trails by double-digit margins 17 days before the election on Nov. 5.

In his radio broadcast, Dole pointed to news reports about hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign contributions to the Democratic National Commitee from people associated with an Indonesian banking firm, a South Korean firm and by people in a Buddhist temple at a Los Angeles fundraiser attended by Vice President Al Gore.
"These efforts were designed to sidestep American campaign laws," said Dole, who charged "some of these actions were probably illegal."
Dole said the contributions "bought access and influence" with top administration officials and Clinton himself who met some of the donors.

"These things, simply stated, are inconsistent with the American tradition," Dole said. "In other countries, such habits of corruption are common. But they must never be allowed to change and distort our political system. We do not import corruption from other nations, we export our vision of democracy to the rest of the world."
Dole said Clinton has refused to explain the activities, although he failed to say there has been no indication that Clinton knew about any of the donations or whether they were improper if he did.
"The ethical vacuum at the heart of this administration has been filled by foreign political money," Dole said.

He conceded "we all make mistakes" in following the complicated campaign laws, but gave Clinton little slack. "The Clinton foreign money scandal is not politics as usual," said Dole. "Taken together, these actions are a singular and serious betrayal of the public trust. We cannot accept this kind of activity is normal or permissible in America without diminishing the ideals of America itself."
He added: "Clinton's silence on these issues of public trust is a form of admission. And our silence would be a form of permission."
